title: Tannin and time
subtitle: Why Nebbiolo needs patience
objectives: Describe how it changes with age

steps.title: Built to last
steps.body: Nebbiolo's very high tannin and acidity make young Barolo and Barbaresco firm, even harsh. Over years, tannins polymerise, linking into longer chains that feel softer. Acidity preserves freshness. Traditionally, Barolo needed 10 years or more before it was ready.

steps.title: How it changes
steps.body: Young Nebbiolo shows red cherry, rose and fresh herbs. With age, it fades to garnet and brick, and develops tar, leather, truffle, dried roses, tobacco and forest floor. The finest can last 30 to 50 years. Modern winemaking has made many approachable sooner, but the best still reward patience.

steps.prompt: What happens to Nebbiolo's tannins over time?
steps.explanation: Tannins bind into longer chains that feel smoother.

steps.body: Decant young Barolo for several hours before serving. Old Barolo needs only a short, gentle decant to remove sediment.

steps.prompt: Order these colours as a Nebbiolo ages.
steps.explanation: Nebbiolo starts pale and turns orange-brown with age.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Nebbiolo's high tannin and acidity need time to soften
With age it develops truffle, tar and dried roses
The finest Barolo lasts 30 to 50 years
